business_items.title: Microsoft: China’s Salt Typhoon hackers are using Artex
business_items.summary: An AI tool implicated in several high-profile breaches is rapidly being integrated into the hacking suites of groups from China and North Korea, Microsoft said.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
An AI tool implicated in several high-profile breaches is rapidly being integrated into the hacking suites of groups from China and North Korea, Microsoft said.

State-backed hacking groups in China and North Korea are using a powerful AI hacking tool in attacks, according to a new report from Microsoft.

Microsoft explained that state-sponsored and financially motivated hackers are using Artex, an AI-powered platform that can automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions at machine speed.

The study emerged hours after The New York Times and NextGov reported that Artex was allegedly used in attacks on the CIA, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

Microsoft said on Wednesday that Chinese state-backed groups Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon have integrated Artex into their suite of tools, using it for “network reconnaissance, credential attacks, and web application exploitation.”

“In the past few weeks, we’ve reported several distinct campaigns that abused Artex to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation,” Microsoft explained.

Salt Typhoon is a prolific Chinese hacking group that U.S. agencies believe was behind the breach of at least nine telecommunications giants in 2024. The hack alarmed White House officials in 2024 because it allegedly gave China’s hackers access to communications from the phones of President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance as well as several Democratic leaders.

Salt Typhoon was also accused of attacking several European governments and critical infrastructure organizations globally .

Artex was released in July, and according to Microsoft, it has been steadily added to the arsenal of multiple North Korean and Chinese groups.

Artex allows threat actors to define specific goals and use AI agents to attack targets. Microsoft said Artex “can advance from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access to a target organization in a matter of minutes.”

“ARTEX does not introduce new attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques. ARTEX does sometimes transmit distinctive characteristics associated with its integrated penetration testing tools,” Microsoft explained.

“However, threat actors using ARTEX can and do vary network indicators like source IP address or user agent string, especially to bypass static or simple signature-based detection and blocking. The most reliable and durable signal of ARTEX activity is behavioral: ARTEX sends a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retries variations on the same technique or moves on to next-stage actions at machine speed.”

By default, Artex does not take measures to hide its activity, the researchers added.

While the Chinese researcher behind the tool initially removed the source code from GitHub last month, other developers made copies , and at least one Chinese company now offers commercial access to a version of it.

Microsoft noted that defenders can tell when Artex is being used based on bursts of machine speed activity and by the “characteristically large volume of anomalous traffic from a single source in a short time.”

The FBI released its own advisory on Artex two weeks ago, warning that it is being used prolifically by cybercriminals and nation-states to breach government agencies and dozens of critical sectors worldwide.

The tool was recently implicated in multiple attacks on South Korean and Japanese financial institutions, causing national scandals in both countries. Microsoft previously said Artex was used by Chinese state-backed actors in a recent supply chain attack on IT management software company ConnectWise .

business_items.title: FIFA says hackers accessed ‘limited set of personal and business information’
business_items.summary: The Switzerland-based international governing body for soccer says it's working with relevant authorities and law enforcement to investigate a recent breach.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The Switzerland-based international governing body for soccer says it's working with relevant authorities and law enforcement to investigate a recent breach.

The Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA) confirmed that internal data was stolen during a recent cyberattack.

The Switzerland-based soccer organization said hackers breached its systems and gained “unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information.”

"FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement,” a spokesperson said.

"FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data. Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned."

The organization did not respond to follow up questions about the nature of the incident. FIFA is the governing body of international soccer and organizes the World Cup, which was held this summer. It has about 700 employees and is headquartered in Zurich.

The Handsome Boy Hacking Club (HBHC) cybercriminal group claimed last week that it stole more than 12 GB of data from the organization and attempted to extort FIFA but failed.

The group eventually published the stolen data on a cybercriminal forum, claiming to have accessed FIFA’s Microsoft environment. The stolen data allegedly includes identity and immigration documents, financial records, legal documents, governance information and more.

The hacking group emerged last week and little is known about its members or associations.

The FIFA incident follows other recent attacks on European soccer leagues. Spain’s top soccer league LaLiga said on Monday that hackers stole personal information belonging to fans in a cyberattack affecting its digital services and those of several Spanish clubs.

In May, Dutch police arrested a 35-year-old man suspected of hacking into the computer systems of Ajax, one of the Netherlands’ most prominent soccer clubs. The French Football Federation also disclosed a cyberattack in 2025.

business_items.title: 1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe
business_items.summary: The password manager maker said an attacker gained access to an employee's corporate account and took some information about customers.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The password manager maker said an attacker gained access to an employee's corporate account and took some information about customers.

Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.

The attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the company’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in.

1Password said that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them.

In addition, the company said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident.

It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident.

1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll update if we hear back from 1Password.

The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts.

business_items.title: DOJ accuses former cyber executive of defrauding ransomware victims by secretly paying hackers
business_items.summary: U.S. prosecutors accused the former executive of defrauding victims of ransomware by paying the hackers, charging victims more, and pocketing the difference.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
U.S. prosecutors accused the former executive of defrauding victims of ransomware by paying the hackers, charging victims more, and pocketing the difference.

The U.S. Department of Justice has indicted a former executive of a ransomware recovery firm after he allegedly defrauded victims of cyberattacks by claiming the company could get their encrypted files back.

According to federal prosecutors , Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, was the chief technology officer at RansomwareHelp, which purported to offer data recovery services to victims of ransomware. The company’s website, which currently reads as “under maintenance,” claimed it could decrypt hacked data by using its proprietary technology, according to an archived copy of the site from earlier this year. RansomwareHelp touted a success rate of “over 99%.”

But the company allegedly had no technical ability to unscramble data and instead “negotiated with and paid a ransom to the ransomware actors to decrypt the victim data,” while charging the ransomware victim more and keeping the difference,” per the Justice Department’s statement.

Palacio Escobar then allegedly used the funds to buy several properties in Florida.

The DOJ said the FBI carried out an undercover operation in June, in part posing as a company that claimed it had been hit by ransomware. The company claimed to the undercover agents that it never negotiated with hackers or paid a ransom. But then Palacio Escobar paid the apparent hackers some $6,000 in cryptocurrency, without the knowledge that FBI agents were also posing as the ransomware hackers.

404 Media first reported the indictment last week against Palacio Escobar. He faces three charges of wire fraud, and could receive 20 years in prison on each count.

Palacio Escobar is the latest, albeit rare, example of cybersecurity professionals going rogue. Earlier this year, two ransomware negotiators working for cybersecurity companies were jailed on hacking and extortion charges, after being caught moonlighting with the ransomware gangs that they were ostensibly investigating. A third ransomware negotiator was also convicted of helping hackers deploy ransomware against several companies.

Last month, independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs reported that FBI agents arrested a Canadian cybersecurity executive in Philadelphia on allegations that he was involved with the theft of FBI personnel records by the hacking and extortion gang ShinyHunters. The hacking group told TechCrunch that they took credit for the theft of FBI data in September, which they said they would not publicly release, a departure from its earlier extortion-based cyberattacks.

The federal charges against the Canadian cybersecurity executive relate to conspiracy to commit extortion, though much of the court docket — and his alleged links to the hacking group — remains under seal.

business_items.title: Florida ransomware recovery CEO indicted for allegedly paying hacker ransoms
business_items.summary: The CEO of a ransomware recovery firm was indicted by a federal grand jury over allegations he lied about his services and paid out ransoms to cybercriminals.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The CEO of a ransomware recovery firm was indicted by a federal grand jury over allegations he lied about his services and paid out ransoms to cybercriminals.

The CEO of a ransomware recovery firm was indicted by a federal grand jury after prosecutors accused him of lying about his services and simply paying out ransoms to cybercriminals.

Colombian national Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, is the co-founder of a company based in Florida that marketed itself as a data recovery service for ransomware victims.

Palacio claimed he had decryption tools that allowed him to help victims without negotiating or paying ransomware gangs. Instead, Palacio allegedly paid ransoms and charged his customers enough to make a profit.

Federal agencies have increasingly sought to crack down on the murky industry of ransomware recovery and cybercriminal mediation in recent months.

“As alleged, the defendant preyed on ransomware victims by falsely marketing a solution he did not possess, secretly negotiating with cybercriminals, and profiting from the difference,” said Charles Calenda, first assistant U.S. attorney.

“Businesses and individuals seeking to recover from a cyberattack should not be victimized for a second time by those they turn to for help.”

He is facing three counts of wire fraud, which carry a maximum sentence of 60 years in prison.

Before the DOJ announced the charges, the news outlet 404 Media and independent journalist Brian Krebs published details of Escobar’s operation, writing that he ran a company called Ransomwarehelp.com. The company’s website currently says it is under maintenance.

On Wednesday, Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva confirmed previous reports that the FBI staged an operation in June where they posed as a ransomware gang and victim.

The FBI went to Palacio for assistance and was told his company “never negotiated with or paid the ransom to ransomware attackers but instead could recover the data through its sophisticated decryption technology.”

“The indictment alleges that despite these representations, Palacio did negotiate with and make a payment in the amount of approximately $6,000 in Bitcoin to the purported ransomware actor, which was also an undercover FBI operative, in exchange for the decryption key,” prosecutors said.

“Palacio charged the undercover company approximately $13,260 for his company’s purported decryption technology services.”

He was arrested in Las Vegas on October 22 before being transferred to Rhode Island. He was released on pretrial bond on November 20.

“As alleged, Mr. Palacio Escobar is the proverbial wolf in sheep’s clothing, representing both himself and his company as experts in data recovery, when all the while he was paying the perpetrators of these ransomware attacks, under the guise of helping his clients,” FBI agent Ted Docks said. “Little did they know he was ripping them off.”

A cybersecurity firm that spoke to Krebs claimed it was hired by a ransomware victim who alleged Palacio had deleted the ransomware notes from its system so that he would be the sole person in charge of communicating with the hackers.

Last month, the DOJ charged another Florida-based owner of a ransomware recovery firm for conducting a similar scheme.

business_items.title: Australia passes tough legislation requiring big tech to preempt foreseeable harms
business_items.summary: The Digital Duty of Care Act sailed through Australia's Parliament. It will mandate that online providers establish protocols to protect users from threats of violence and rape as well as behavior that could cause significant harms.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The Digital Duty of Care Act sailed through Australia's Parliament. It will mandate that online providers establish protocols to protect users from threats of violence and rape as well as behavior that could cause significant harms.

Australia’s Parliament on Wednesday greenlit legislation creating sweeping online safety reforms that open the possibility of billions of dollars in fines for big tech companies that fail to preempt online harms before they occur.

Known as the Digital Duty of Care Act, the legislation sailed through Parliament with strong backing from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

His administration has been a global leader in fighting against online safety harms and spearheaded Australia’s pioneering strict age requirements for social media use that took effect in December 2025 and have since been copied by governments worldwide.

The pending law will mandate that online providers establish protocols to ensure Australians are protected from threats of violence and rape as well as behavior that could cause significant harms.

Platforms are required to detect and decrease risks from harmful content and must bolster protections for users under 18 against pornography, suicide and eating disorders. They also must undertake annual written risk assessments and call out major platform design changes such as endless scrolling that create new harms.

Under the law, users also will be able to opt out of algorithmic feeds and will be required to prove their age to access porn.

After the law passed, Albanese reportedly told Parliament it will be a “powerful instrument to protect our children and our society from online harms by placing the onus on the tech platforms to ensure a safer online environment.”

“This is a victory for our children and young people. The dangers were unforeseen when the digital world was young,” Albanese said. “But now that the digital world has matured, they can be easily recognized and they can be remedied.”

Similar legislation is already in place in the U.K. and European Union . A bill seeking to impose a duty of care against large platforms has been introduced by U.S. lawmakers but has stagnated in Congress.

U.S. officials have accused the Australian legislation of violating free speech, threatening American companies’ business models and imposing vague requirements that will cause tech giants to overhaul their services to avoid liability.

“We are particularly concerned by potential mandates that would allow regulators to impose rigid, one-size-fits-all platform design requirements – such as forced chronological feeds or opt-in recommendation systems,” the U.S. Embassies and Consulates in Australia said in a September public comment .

The legislation does not undermine free speech, Albanese told Parliament in October, saying that “rather than someone in the United States deciding” what people see, now Australians can “decide themselves.”

The law will require platforms to “give us more choice over the content and the features that we use, including the feeds that we choose,” Albanese said.

business_items.title: Allstate suffers multiday tech outage ahead of Thanksgiving
business_items.summary: The disruption comes at a particularly bad time for the insurance giant, as millions of Americans prepare to travel for the Thanksgiving holiday weekend.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The disruption comes at a particularly bad time for the insurance giant, as millions of Americans prepare to travel for the Thanksgiving holiday weekend.

U.S. insurer Allstate has been experiencing a tech outage since Monday morning, leaving customers nationwide unable to access their accounts, review their policy information, file claims, pay their bills, and more, just ahead of the U.S. Thanksgiving holidays.

The outage has been impacting both the company’s website and mobile app, TechCrunch confirmed.

The breakdown follows a report from earlier this month that Allstate was planning to lay off up to 10% of its staff as part of an AI-driven efficiency push. (The company had not confirmed the report, which was attributed to unnamed sources.)

Allstate’s outage is the latest in a series of disruptions to services such as Microsoft Outlook and Teams , the airlines , Apple Pay, and several banks. Trump administration officials have said the outages are not being caused by cyberattacks, but are rather being caused by a recent set of upgrades to systems, many of which run on older technology. Those systems are now in need of more frequent security and bug fixes as AI makes it easier and faster to discover vulnerabilities.

At present, a message on Allstate’s website advises customers trying to log in that its services aren’t available, and that the company is “working to restore access as soon as possible.” On X, Allstate is employing what appear to be automated replies to customer complaints , asking them to DM the Allstate account with more information.

Downdetector , a crowdsourced outage-reporting website, shows users began reporting Allstate’s outage from Monday morning. However, the company hasn’t yet issued a formal statement about the disruption, what’s causing it, or when it may be resolved. In the meantime, local insurance agents have been fielding calls and emails from customers who aren’t able to use the company’s online services.

The timing of the outage is particularly bad given that Thanksgiving is a big travel holiday in the U.S., which means there will be car accidents. Customers will be left without a way to get in touch with their auto insurer to file claims and get roadside assistance through Allstate’s app.

Allstate did not immediately return a request for comment. On Wednesday evening, after publication, the company sent the following statement (below). It did not answer questions about the outage’s cause or planned resolution.

Allstate customers can reach us in many ways, including online, by phone and through local offices. Some access has been restricted over the last 48 hours, but we continue to be available for customers and respond to and settle claims. To the extent service interruptions impact a customer’s ability to make a payment, they won’t lose coverage or be charged late fees.

business_items.title: Todoist confirms 6% of customers’ details were stolen in data breach
business_items.summary: Todoist said a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Todoist said a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates.

Task management app Todoist said on Tuesday that a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates. The company said around 6% of its customers were affected and blamed stolen credentials for the breach.

Todoist said the attacker used stolen credentials to access the company’s version control system and source code between November 22 and 23. The hacker then changed employee access controls and reached the app’s cloud infrastructure via an employee’s work account.

The hacker downloaded credentials of early Todoist users whose passwords were stored using an older hashing method, but didn’t change any source code, the company said. Todoist said it has blocked the attack path and reset passwords as a mitigation step, as well as disabled the Todoist for Outlook email add-on.

For a small number of people, about 0.001% of its userbase, the hacker also searched through tasks, comments, and attachment names to look for credentials for other services, like API keys and access tokens.

The hacker also pulled Todoist API tokens and Slack integration tokens, and looked for emails, addresses, and attachment file names through the Todoist for Outlook extension if it was connected to accounts and had permission to read emails.

The company said it has sent a notice to those affected and asked them to reset their credentials and change their login details in other places with the same password. The company is asking users to also update API tokens, reconnect integrations, and revoke or replace any access keys, recovery phrases, or credentials they had stored in Todoist comments.

Todoist said it has also reset its internal access structure and how remote command execution works in its cloud environment to prevent such incidents in the future.

Todoist’s founder and CEO Amir Salihefendić apologized to users about the incident on X , and said the company will take a closer look at why it happened.

The to-do app’s data breach is the latest in a burgeoning list of data breaches in which hackers use stolen credentials to access data and systems at enterprises. So far this year, we’ve seen several companies fall victim to this form of attack, including Uber and Klue .

business_items.title: Suspected ransomware attack disrupts cancer treatments, surgeries at Guadeloupe hospital
business_items.summary: France’s national cybersecurity agency is investigating a suspected ransomware attack that impaired the computer systems of the University Hospital of Guadeloupe, forcing doctors to postpone surgeries, suspend some cancer treatments and revert to pen and paper.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
France’s national cybersecurity agency is investigating a suspected ransomware attack that impaired the computer systems of the University Hospital of Guadeloupe, forcing doctors to postpone surgeries, suspend some cancer treatments and revert to pen and paper.

France’s national cybersecurity agency, known as ANSSI, said Tuesday the incident appeared to involve ransomware and that investigators were examining whether hackers gained access to the hospital’s systems through an unnamed IT supplier that was reportedly compromised several months ago.

French prosecutors have launched a criminal investigation into the incident. It remains unclear who was behind the attack. The hospital’s management told local media on Monday that it had not received a ransom demand and ruled out paying a ransom.

The hospital — the largest on the French Caribbean island of approximately 380,000 residents — said on its website it had canceled some surgical procedures, medical consultations and imaging tests through at least Friday.

Radiation therapy has been temporarily suspended over safety concerns, while chemotherapy sessions scheduled for Monday were canceled. The hospital is reviewing upcoming appointments based on each patient’s medical needs.

Emergency services, dialysis treatments and urgent cardiac procedures remain available. The hospital has asked residents to visit its emergency departments only if they need immediate medical care.

Hospital employees first experienced computer and telephone outages on Saturday evening, according to local media reports. What initially appeared to be a technical malfunction turned out to be a cyberattack that encrypted the hospital’s databases.

“We’re back to pen and paper, relying on couriers who travel from one department to another,” the hospital’s director told local media.

As of Tuesday, healthcare workers were still unable to access patients’ electronic medical records and were manually processing prescriptions and collecting laboratory results, slowing patient care.

The hospital has encouraged patients to bring paper copies of their medical records, prescriptions and previous test results to appointments.

It remains unclear whether the hackers stole any personal or medical information. The hospital said it would notify anyone whose data was compromised and warned patients to watch out for phishing attempts by criminals posing as hospital staff.

The hospital plans to gradually restore the affected systems after checking them for malware. Recovery is expected to take several days, but it remains unclear when normal operations will fully resume.

The attack came as the hospital was relocating its operations to a new facility in Belle-Plaine. The French government financed the construction of the new hospital after a major fire damaged its previous facilities in 2017.

According to hospital management, the new facility’s computer systems have stronger security protections, making the disruption easier to manage there. Despite the attack, the hospital has maintained its plans to transfer pediatric emergency services to the new site.

Two other French healthcare organizations — Bordeaux University Hospital and France’s National Cancer Institute — disclosed cyberattacks earlier this week.

Bordeaux University Hospital said it discovered its computer systems had been compromised after detecting that two of its email accounts had been used to send mass emails to employees.

A threat actor known as Scarlettgroup claimed responsibility for the breach, threatening to publish allegedly stolen medical records, prescriptions, laboratory results and financial documents.

The hospital has not confirmed the hackers’ claims and is investigating whether any information was stolen. It temporarily restricted external access to one of its servers as a precaution but said the incident had not disrupted patient care.

business_items.title: FinCEN investigates cybersecurity incident, takes systems offline
business_items.summary: The Treasury financial intelligence unit said the filing portal remains operational, and deadlines for affected filers have been extended. The post FinCEN investigates cybersecurity incident, takes systems offline appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Treasury’s FinCEN took systems offline to investigate an unauthorized intrusion while keeping its Bank Secrecy Act filing portal operational.

The Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network is investigating a cybersecurity incident in which an unauthorized party gained access to a limited subset of its systems, the agency said in a notice posted to its Bank Secrecy Act filing portal.

FinCEN, the federal government’s financial intelligence unit, said it took some systems offline as a precaution while the investigation continues. The agency did not say how the intrusion occurred, how long it lasted or who was behind it. A source told CyberScoop that the FBI, CISA, and third-party forensic examiners are working to determine the scope and impact of the incident. As of today, there is no evidence of any breach of beneficial ownership databases.

The BSA E-Filing System, the portal at the center of the disruption, is FinCEN’s web-based platform for submitting reports required under the Bank Secrecy Act, the 1970 law that forms the backbone of U.S. anti-money-laundering policy. Banks, credit unions, brokerages, casinos and other financial institutions use it to transmit suspicious activity reports, currency transaction reports and related filings electronically through a secure network.

FinCEN said the filing website itself remains operational, though some services may be temporarily unavailable. The agency said it is extending deadlines for filers affected by the disruption.

The agency also said its Financial Institutions Hotline is unaffected by the disruption and remains available to financial institutions that need to expedite delivery of suspicious activity information to law enforcement.

The incident places a temporary strain on infrastructure that the financial sector relies on to meet statutory reporting obligations. Suspicious activity reports filed through the system feed the database that FinCEN uses to support criminal, tax and national security investigations, and delays in filings can slow the flow of information to federal authorities.

It was not immediately clear how long the affected systems would remain offline. FinCEN said it is working to return all systems to normal operations as soon as possible. The agency has not said whether any data was taken or altered.

The incident was announced the same day the CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence discovered a data breach of an open-source intelligence analysis system. It is unclear if the two incidents are related.

business_items.title: Unclassified intel system hit by hackers, affecting CIA, ODNI
business_items.summary: CyberScoop confirmed the incident, with a source saying “no other systems are currently at risk.” The post Unclassified intel system hit by hackers, affecting CIA, ODNI appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence confirmed a data breach affecting an unclassified open-source intelligence system.

The CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence have discovered a data breach of an open-source intelligence analysis system, CyberScoop has confirmed.

The New York Times first reported the breach Tuesday, writing that the breach had exposed some unclassified information. A source familiar with the breach said there was a disruption, but the exposure was limited.

‘The hack did not involve our classified networks or classified information, and no other systems are currently at risk,” the source said.

The discovery is the latest in a series of intrusions affecting U.S. security agencies, including two at the FBI and another at the National Security Agency .

Ben Bernstein, manager of cybersecurity advisers at Huntress, said in an emailed comment that while the reported breach didn’t hit classified data, open-source (OSINT) information can still be sensitive.

“Calling this ‘unclassified’ doesn’t make it harmless,” he said. “These systems pull in public and commercial info like news, satellite imagery, and paid data feeds, so the raw material isn’t a state secret. The value for an adversary is seeing what the CIA and ODNI are doing with it.”

“If you can see what analysts are searching for and what topics they’re tracking, you get a solid look at U.S. intelligence priorities and blind spots without ever touching a classified file,” he continued. “These OSINT networks are also tough to secure because they have to stay open to the public internet to do their job.”

The CIA declined to comment and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.

business_items.title: Maple raises $5.3M to build AI products that protect your data, even from itself
business_items.summary: The startup's encrypted AI architecture is designed to prevent even the company itself from accessing users' private data.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The startup's encrypted AI architecture is designed to prevent even the company itself from accessing users' private data.

As AI assistants evolve into more capable agents that can access our files, emails, calendar, browser, and more, the amount of trust we’re expected to place in AI companies is growing. One startup called Maple , co-founded by a former Apple engineer who worked on privacy-preserving technologies, is taking a different approach with its AI app, where users’ data remains private — even from the company itself.

“We wanted to build something that was not only encrypted but also could be proven, and that people could go look at the open-source code, and then they could look at what we call trusted execution environments,” explains Maple co-founder and CEO Mark Suman . “They can look at and verify the code that’s running on our servers, so they don’t really have to take our word for it.”

“They can audit everything themselves and know how their data is being handled,” he adds.

The idea of trust is Maple’s larger theme, as the startup proposes that there’s a way to build an AI app where consumers don’t have to trade privacy for convenience, as its competitors often require with their invasive privacy policies and data collection practices , and sometimes even training on users’ personal data .

Instead of asking users to trust that Maple won’t misuse their personal data, it’s attempting to build a business where it can’t access that data in the first place.

Like other AI apps on the market, Maple allows users to engage in a chat experience where they ask questions and get answers. Meanwhile, its newly launched desktop app, Maple Work , offers a more agentic experience where the AI can control your computer, work with your files and apps, and control your browser to get online tasks handled.

With the company’s recently closed $5.3 million round, it’s moving on to its next product — a cloud-based agent that will be able to continue its work even if your computer isn’t on. This addition would make Maple more competitive with other popular consumer AI services, like Meta’s Muse , Instinct , and other AI agents that work over chat.

The oversubscribed seed round was led by Epic Ventures, with participation from Draper Associates, Planetary VC, and Epoch VC, and follows a pre-seed angel round of under a million. Maple plans to raise a Series A in the first half of 2027, given the investor interest.

Suman, who previously spent six years at Apple, already had a background where AI and privacy overlapped, he tells TechCrunch.

At Apple, he worked on AI and machine learning with a particular focus on computer vision. Given Apple’s stance on consumer privacy, the challenge he faced was building products that would protect people’s identity while benefiting from computer vision techniques. His co-founder, Anthony Ronning (CTO), has a background in defense tech, security, and networking.

Ronning started the company that later became Maple AI back in 2023, initially as a privacy-focused fintech. When Suman teamed up with Ronning in August 2024, the idea to create Maple AI was born. The following January, the product became available to the public as a mobile app.

The app offers a familiar interface for those used to AI chatbots, but under the hood it runs a variety of open models, including versions of DeepSeek , Kimi , GLM , Inkling from Thinking Machines, Google’s Gemma , and OpenAI’s GPT OSS . Users can pick and choose the models they want or, for a simpler experience, just toggle between a quick model and the more powerful one.

The models themselves run inside a trusted execution environment (TEE) — meaning a server with hardware encryption on it — within a U.S.-based data center. (Maple also offers support for European customers through a partner that runs its server in Europe.)

“We actually don’t have access to [the data] while it’s inside the TEE,” explains Suman. “The data gets encrypted first on your device using a unique password that’s only known by you, the user — we don’t have access to it. It then goes into this TEE, and it gets decrypted inside there. The AI does its thing, and then it re-encrypts it with your password and sends it back to you,” he continues. “So we provide an end-to-end experience that’s very easy for the user, but we actually don’t have access to the raw data as it’s in flight or even when it’s at rest,” he adds.

This allows Maple to protect its users’ data, even from outsiders — like if hackers breached its system or the government came with a subpoena, for instance. All it could do would be to hand over an encrypted file.

“We just simply don’t want access to it,” Suman says of customers’ data. “That’s not part of our business model. And we also don’t want it to be part of our threat model.”

With the new desktop app, Maple is looking to small businesses that may want to benefit from AI without the data privacy risks. Inside the app, there’s an integration store where users can connect with other apps, like their Gmail or calendar. The desktop app can also spin up a subagent that works inside another AI app you may have on your desktop, like Claude, Codex, or others that support the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). This allows customers to use their preferred AI app for specific tasks, without having to give it all their information — just what’s needed for the given task.

Next year, Maple plans to enter the enterprise market with pilot work, where it will offer its own version of zero data retention. (Maple doesn’t retain most of the customers’ data, but when it has to, that data is encrypted.) It’s now in the process of completing SOC 2 compliance and security audits to get ready for this expansion.

business_items.summary: Iran is the chief suspect behind the dozens of cyberattacks targeting oil and chemical shipping vessels.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Iran is the chief suspect behind the dozens of cyberattacks targeting oil and chemical shipping vessels.

U.S. officials suspect Iranian hackers may be behind as many as 50 cyberattacks targeting shipping vessels in recent weeks, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal .

The ships carrying oil, liquefied gas, and other explosive chemicals were hacked as they traveled across Asia and Europe. Several oil tankers headed toward the U.S. coast in August also had their navigation systems breached, prompting cybersecurity teams within the FBI and Coast Guard to board the vessels.

The report said officials are investigating if Iran is expanding its recent wave of hacks against the U.S. by targeting large vessels to sow fear among shippers, disrupt routes, or to cause an explosion at a port. (Ships have backup controls in the event that automated systems are hacked or fail.)

Hackers may have been abusing a bug dubbed FortiBleed , which allows hackers to break into networks by compromising vulnerable Fortinet-made routers. A joint FBI-Coast Guard security alert from September warned that Fortinet routers are used on shipping vessels.

Iran has been firing back on all sides since the start of the U.S./Israel-led war earlier this year, which killed the country’s supreme leader. Many of Iran’s retaliations have been in the form of cyberattacks, with U.S. officials blaming Iran for hacks targeting hundreds of American water providers and U.S. medical tech companies .

A spokesperson for the FBI did not respond to a request for comment about the shipping hacks or whether it had a more accurate figure.

business_items.title: UK warns AI-driven cyberattacks are exposing years of weak security
business_items.summary: The British cyber agency says that "building strong foundations has never mattered more" as AI hacking tools rely on exploiting simple security flaws.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The British cyber agency says that "building strong foundations has never mattered more" as AI hacking tools rely on exploiting simple security flaws.

The U.K. government’s cybersecurity unit says it has seen a “marked rise” in AI-driven cyberattacks in recent months, as hackers increasingly rely on autonomous hacking tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to break into systems and networks.

The U.K. National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) said it has seen several cyber incidents since September involving autonomous hacking tools, such as penetration testing tools used by defenders to stress-test their cybersecurity defenses. These incidents have caused intrusions at organizations and resulted in downtime, the unit said in a blog post .

The NCSC says that while none of the vulnerabilities being exploited are new, the speed at which these AI tools are able to carry out simple hacks has changed.

The rise in AI-related cyberattacks coincides with the broader release earlier this year of open source autonomous penetration testing tools like Artex and Cairn, among others, which anyone can download and use at no cost. The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation recently warned that malicious hackers are using AI penetration testing tools to carry out cyberattacks at unprecedented speeds.

While cyberattacks and intrusions are on the rise, the message from London is that many of these attacks are preventable with basic cybersecurity defenses and best practices.

“Notably, the issues being exploited currently are not novel memory corruption vulnerabilities (or even known but unpatched vulnerabilities), but unmitigated weaknesses that are often the result of years of technical debt that organisations have accumulated,” the NCSC wrote.

The unit said that agentic hacking tools often look for exposed or internet-facing systems, then quickly run through lists of weak or easy-to-guess passwords or abuse API endpoints often used by developers to access data.

The NCSC said that AI “does not make established cyber security controls obsolete,” but rather that “building strong foundations has never mattered more.”

The unit added that AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities and faster to exploit them, warning that weaknesses that have gone unnoticed for years can now be found in minutes.

business_items.details:
FBI Director Kash Patel declined to share details on the National Crime Information Center hack, citing an active investigation into the breach.

There’s an active investigation into a hack of the FBI’s National Crime Information Center, bureau director Kash Patel said Tuesday, but he otherwise declined to comment on details of the breach.

Patel said “the matter is ongoing” when asked at a new conference about who was behind the hack reported Friday and what information they obtained from the NCIC, a national database for sharing information on warrants, fugitives, missing persons and background checks.

“We’ve publicly released, as we always do, information we are permitted to at this time, but it’s an ongoing investigation,” he said, adding that the FBI was working with other agencies on the matter. “So we’re working with the interagency, and as we’ve done in the past, we will make all the information public either through our partners at the Department of Justice or through our engagements on Capitol Hill.”

President Donald Trump over the weekend said the breach was “not good” and that he’d just learned about it, but otherwise downplayed it, something he often does in response to cyberattacks against the United States.

“I don’t like that,” Trump said. “But maybe we will learn things that we would’ve never learned otherwise.”

It was the second breach in recent months at the FBI, which suffered an attack from ShinyHunters in September that saw the bureau’s website defaced and the hacking group claiming it stole sensitive information on FBI agents and jobseekers.

Patel made his remarks at a Justice Department press conference to tout progress in its battle against scammers — including cybercrime — since Trump signed an executive order in March. As part of his answer to the question about the FBI breach, Patel claimed intrusions were “down 36% based on FBI caseload” under Trump compared to his predecessor, Joe Biden.

business_items.title: UK cyber agency, threat companies tracking rise in AI-assisted hacks
business_items.summary: The National Cyber Security Centre said it is observing a “marked” increase in such attacks across sectors, as threat actors increasingly delegate to machines. The post UK cyber agency, threat companies tracking rise in AI-assisted hacks appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre warns of a marked rise in fast, low-cost AI-assisted cyberattacks using agentic offensive frameworks.

As U.S. policymakers focus on outages that appear partly caused by widespread patching of AI-identified vulnerabilities, the U.K.’s top cyber intelligence agency says it is seeing more cyberattacks carried out with AI assistance.

On Tuesday, three officials from the National Cyber Security Centre said they had observed “a marked rise” in AI-assisted cyberattacks since September.

“Organizations across multiple sectors are reporting incidents as a result of threat actors using ‘agentic offensive frameworks’; software originally designed for red teaming being applied beyond its defensive purpose,” wrote David Chismon, chief technology officer for architecture, and two partially-named NCSC staffers, Kris B., incident handler, and Ellen T, lead data scientist on the vulnerability management team.

The incidents resemble past AI-enabled hacks, defined by rapid, automated vulnerability discovery and attempted exploitation of all of a target’s internet-facing assets “in quick succession.” The impact on victims ranged from outages to system compromise.

“What has changed, is how quickly and persistently threat actors can conduct attacks – at low cost – using these frameworks combined with cheap, capable open models or illegal API resellers,” the officials wrote.

The NCSC officials called the threat sobering but noted that “none” of the vulnerabilities or attacks are novel. They’re known weaknesses that organizations should have patched sooner, and most can still be patched. Additionally, hacking operations moving at speed and scale generate a great deal of “noise” and telemetry that defenders can track.

Large language models are powerful on their own, but combined with technical harnesses , offensive security frameworks , and human expertise, they can become genuine national security threats.

Technical harnesses – systems and tools that can guide and contextualize LLM-driven actions, manage memory and resource requirements, and dictate when human operators need to step in – are particularly valuable to both cybersecurity defenders and malicious hackers.

Eric Loui, a principal intelligence analyst at CrowdStrike, said the company is tracking dozens of threat actor groups that increasingly delegate decisions to agentic AI. Sophisticated harnesses means that even easily accessible open-source LLMs, like Chinese-made DeepSeek, can become powerful offensive hacking tools in the right hands.

“These are older models, the safeguards are easy to overcome,” Loui said last week at the CYBERWARCON hacker conference in Arlington, Va. “And you know, in the worst-case scenario you can just start a new session and try, try again and that worked well enough” for many threat actors.

In one attack on a healthcare organization in Argentina, the threat actor identified the target and asked the model to find an initial access point. Loui emphasized how rudimentary the instructions were.

“They don’t tell it to go after the services, they don’t tell it how to do the recon,” he said. “They just trust that the harness [and] the training data in the AI model are sufficient, and then after 90 minutes the agent has identified and exploited a SQL injection vulnerability and [is] able to get it checked.”

Other threat analysts told CyberScoop they’ve observed hackers increasingly building bespoke software and malware for each engagement. That makes it harder to identify threat actors by their toolsets or track malware “families,” as threat intelligence companies have traditionally done.

The NCSC and many cybersecurity experts have said these vulnerabilities reflect decades of accumulated technical debt, leaving them outdated, insecure and unmonitored assets to manage.

As AI tools become more accessible and cheaper , offensive security faces no meaningful financial or resource constraints when determining targets.

Some, like former NSA cybersecurity director Rob Joyce, liken the coming years of exploitation and patching to a forest fire: widespread damage that also clears the brush that makes such fires so dangerous. Organizations that address built-up technical debt, through proactive patching or in response to malicious hacks, may emerge with more secure and resilient systems.

“Nearly everything the NCSC has seen can be prevented by implementing cyber security best practice, the application of modern cyber security approaches like zero trust and by the diligent application of technical controls in line with your organization’s technologies and processes,” the NCSC officials wrote.

business_items.title: Tomorrow’s quantum threat is today’s open door
business_items.summary: Post-quantum cryptography deserves a place on the roadmap. But in operational technology, the threats doing damage today are far more basic, and far more urgent. The post Tomorrow’s quantum threat is today’s open door appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
OT leaders should prioritize network segmentation, asset inventory, and basic security controls before chasing post-quantum cryptography.

Earlier this month, attackers switched refrigeration systems in supermarkets across nine European countries into defrost mode . Stores were forced to throw out spoiled stock, and as is now being reported, some blood banks in France were hit as well. Around the same time, U.S. agencies including the FBI and CISA warned that internet-exposed refrigeration and temperature controllers were being actively targeted.

The attackers didn’t get in by breaking encryption or cracking passwords. They found admin interfaces exposed to the internet that never should have been public facing, along with known vulnerabilities and, in some cases, default credentials. In other words, unnecessary attack surfaces, unpatched systems, and factory default passwords. They didn’t need a quantum cryptography breakthrough. They had an open door.

That’s worth keeping in mind as the post-quantum cryptography (PQC) conversation picks up speed. New algorithms have been standardized , governments are setting migration timelines , and vendors are urging organizations to start migrating. Quantum computing’s potential to break widely used encryption deserves serious preparation. But nearly all of that guidance is targeted at IT. In operational technology (OT), the PQC timeline looks very different, and the risks hurting organizations today are frankly much lower-hanging fruit.

Before worrying about tomorrow’s lockpick technology, lock today’s open doors.

The devices that run water, electric, critical infrastructure, and manufacturing environments were built for a different era and a different purpose. Some examples are PLCs (programmable logic controllers), HMIs (human-machine interfaces) and OITs (operator interface terminals), as well as RTUs (remote terminal units) and PMRs (pole-mounted routers) in the electric sector.

Start with lifecycles. NIST’s “Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security” (SP 800-82 Rev. 3) notes that OT technology often remains deployed for 10 to 15 years, and sometimes longer. In practice, it’s often much longer. Organizations don’t always inventory these devices, or even realize they’re on the network, so they can sit in public-sector environments for 20 years or more. I’m a millennial, and I’ve assessed equipment at an electrical site that was last updated before I was born.

Then there’s the hardware factor. OT devices are purpose-built to do exactly what they need to do and nothing more. Many run on less than 1 gigabyte of RAM, and some on 512 MB or less. Many don’t support current encryption standards and still rely on protocols and encryption methods that are a decade old or more. Post-quantum algorithms would ask more from hardware that can already barely handle its workload.

These devices aren’t ready for today’s security landscape, let alone tomorrow’s.

Over the years, I’ve assessed more than 35 utility sites and dozens of manufacturing plants. Only a handful had OT networks I’d consider mature or hardened, with clear governance, documented policies and procedures, and controls that held up under testing. Most shared the same weaknesses: default credentials, little or no segmentation, insecure protocols, incomplete asset inventories, and missing policies and procedures. I can say with confidence that fewer than 20% of utilities are ready for a genuine penetration test by today’s standards, let alone a quantum-capable adversary.

None of those gaps are cryptographic. They’re foundational, and they’re the same gaps attackers used in the refrigeration attacks. When a device can be reached from the internet and logged into with a factory password, the strength of its encryption doesn’t matter.

For much of OT, the threat isn’t a future adversary decrypting traffic. It’s a present-day adversary reading cleartext traffic or using a default credential to authenticate to a device that corporate security didn’t even know was connected to the wider internet.

The classic CIA triad is often helpful to keep in mind—it defines three core components of security: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Historically, uptime and safety requirements have pushed OT manufacturers to prioritize availability and integrity, giving confidentiality (encryption) less attention. Confidentiality is more often than not Velcroed onto these devices to meet contract requirements.

Even when confidentiality is considered, many legacy OT devices lack the processing power, memory, or upgrade paths needed to adopt post-quantum cryptography. Newer devices may be better equipped, but long replacement cycles and demanding validation requirements mean OT’s transition to PQC could lag IT’s by years, or even decades.

Additionally, to further mitigate risk, consider that many PLCs and HMIs don’t need direct outbound access. Limit them to strictly what they need. Border gateways and firewalls between environments are great. For legacy devices, go further: consider truly air-gapping them, or placing them in segments with no or extremely limited outbound access. Data diodes, gateways that let data flow in only one direction, are a strong option for getting information out of OT without opening a path back in.

Understanding what you have, making security a focus point of purchasing decisions, implementing basic OT security controls via a mappable framework, and writing associated policies, procedures, etc. is the best way to protect your OT environment.

If I had to pick three priorities for the year ahead, they’d be these. First, segment your networks. If an attacker in your IT environment can reach OT, you have a problem. While you’re at it, remove unnecessary internet exposure, especially admin interfaces, and change every default credential you find. Second, build a complete asset inventory. You can’t protect what you don’t know you have. Invest in a platform, and keep inventory of both hardware and software, especially the devices that have quietly been in service for decades. Finally, run tabletop exercises. Practice what we preach. Test your incident response and recovery capabilities for real, not just on paper. Update your policies, procedures, and playbooks with the lessons learned.

What about procurement? Some guidance suggests writing PQC readiness into OT purchasing requirements today. I’d advise against it. No OT vendor is ready for PQC, and no vendor can credibly assure anything about a threat we haven’t yet seen in action. Make it known that PQC is on your roadmap and ask your vendors about theirs. But don’t select a vendor purely on PQC claims. Put that energy into today’s hard-to-achieve OT challenges instead, like zero trust.

Quantum computing inspires anxiety, and its potential impact on encryption is real. But quantum readiness is a long-term responsibility. Closing obvious security gaps is an immediate need. Companies must do both and stop letting tomorrow’s threat overshadow today’s failures.

Virginia and Oregon attorneys general sued SpaceX and Elon Musk, alleging Grok allowed users to create nonconsensual deepfake nudes.

Two new lawsuits accuse SpaceX and its subsidiaries of violating state consumer and trade laws by allowing its AI tool, Grok, to create deepfake nudes of millions of people earlier this year.

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, both Democrats, filed the lawsuits. They allege SpaceX and owner Elon Musk repeatedly failed to block Grok’s nudification feature after it became clear the tool was being used to break the law by creating nude or defamatory images of real people. The attorneys general want a court to bar SpaceX from advertising or profiting from the tool’s capabilities, pay restitution to victims and impose civil penalties.

“Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false,” Jones said in a statement. “Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children. Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation. The law applies to everyone, and this office will hold big tech accountable when they break the law.”

The lawsuits say Grok launched when other AI companies already knew about the harms of deepfake pornography to adults and children. Many of those companies built safeguards to keep their models from generating such content. Musk, by contrast, is facing separate lawsuits from former victims of child sexual abuse material. Those plaintiffs allege Grok can easily nudify children because it was partly trained on real abuse material found online.

“Led by founder Elon Musk, Defendants chose to ignore this growing industry concern, and instead saw a market opportunity for more profits,” the lawsuit alleged. “To push its lagging product, Grok, to tens of millions of new users, it stripped out industry-standard safeguards and marketed a ‘spicy mode’ built to produce nudity.”

As CyberScoop reported last year, Musk’s public statements and decisions to maintain Grok’s capabilities were so brazen that cybersecurity and privacy lawyers predicted he would face an avalanche of criminal and civil actions . Over the past six months, lawsuits, federal and state investigations, and international regulatory scrutiny have battered the company.

The lawsuits allege that “weak safeguards were not a failure but a feature” of Musk’s business strategy for Grok. Those weak safeguards became one of Grok’s main selling points, marketed as a way to set it apart from other competing AI models.

The lawsuits cite Musk’s own behavior and statements as evidence that he knew about the controversy and often embraced it. He has posted or commented on Grok-altered images of himself and household objects in bikinis. At times, Musk has claimed Grok only alters images to show people in bikinis, or that deepfake pornography is protected free speech under the First Amendment.

The states also claim integrating Grok directly into the social media site X gave users the ability to create abuse material on command, as well as an instant, worldwide distribution platform for it.

Oregon’s lawsuit was brought under the Oregon Unlawful Trade Practices Act, which prohibits misrepresenting a product’s or service’s characteristics, benefits or qualities. The state alleges SpaceX violated the law “by failing to disclose Grok’s known material defects; and by employing unconscionable tactics in connection with selling and distributing Grok and X.”

Virginia’s lawsuit cites violation of the Virginia Consumer Protection Act, the state’s primary law, which prohibits businesses from misrepresenting the source, characteristics or quality of their goods or services.

CyberScoop has reached out to SpaceX for comment on the lawsuits.

business_items.title: Indicted Kosovo credit card theft suspect extradited to US
business_items.summary: Authorities say a hard drive in the possession of Hektor Avdyli contained millions of payment card numbers. The post Indicted Kosovo credit card theft suspect extradited to US appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Hektor Avdyli, a 21-year-old from Kosovo found with 2.7 million payment card numbers, was extradited to the U.S. to face federal credit card fraud charges.

A Kosovo man accused of selling stolen credit card and personal information over the internet, who was allegedly found with millions of payment card numbers in his possession, was extradited to the United States, the Justice Department announced Monday.

In October 2025, a federal grand jury in Wisconsin returned an eight-count indictment charging Hektor Avdyli, 21 — reportedly the nephew of a former member of Kosovo’s parliament — with wire fraud, access device fraud and aggravated identity theft.

Kosovar authorities arrested him in July at the behest of the FBI and DOJ, and he’s now in Milwaukee awaiting trial.

“Unfortunately, there is nothing remotely unusual about American consumers having their identities and financial information stolen online, often by foreign actors,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Brad Schimel for the Eastern District of Wisconsin. “It happens countless times every day, and that theft costs American consumers billions of dollars.”

Avdyli allegedly used online criminal forums to ply his illicit trade, advertising and selling stolen credit card data and personal information to help customers commit fraud. Court documents say that he claimed to steal the information from shopping websites using malware.

As part of the operation to apprehend him, the FBI secretly bought more than 27,000 credit card numbers and related personal information from a seller. The bureau then identified Avdyli as the culprit through its investigative work.

A hard drive in his possession at the time of his arrest had 2.7 million payment card numbers on it, according to authorities.

“FBI Milwaukee worked across international borders to target the criminal actor behind a cybercrime scheme that enabled fraud against American people to include citizens of Wisconsin,” said Special-Agent-in-Charge Alan Karr of FBI Milwaukee.

business_items.title: Kirsten Davies to become national cyber director nominee, Jay Clayton takes acting director job
business_items.summary: After a brief stint as acting director, Davies will become the pick to succeed Sean Cairncross and National Cyber Director Clayton will do double duty. The post Kirsten Davies to become national cyber director nominee, Jay Clayton takes acting director job appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Kirsten Davies and Jay Clayton take on new roles in a federal cyber leadership shuffle following Sean Cairncross's exit as national cyber director.

President Donald Trump will nominate Kirsten Davies for permanent national cyber director, giving the acting role she just received last week for the post to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton pending her confirmation.

A White House official told CyberScoop Monday that “following the overwhelming support Kirsten received from industry and across government after Thursday’s announcement, President Trump has decided to nominate her to serve as national cyber director.”

Davies, in the meantime, will serve as senior adviser for the Office of the National Cyber Director. The same person cannot serve in the acting role of a position while also being the nominee for it.

The move is one of several in a recent federal cyber leadership shuffle, all following the November elections that saw Democrats take control of the House and Senate.

The departure of Sean Cairncross as Trump’s national cyber director opened up his job. Davies was the chief information officer at the Department of Defense prior to receiving the acting national cyber director position, in addition to a background of holding leading cyber roles at big companies like Siemens and Estée Lauder.

Trump also nominated Palantir CISO Michael LoSapio for permanent director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency following the election, although multiple senators have already placed holds on his nomination that look to delay his confirmation until next year — and that’s only if he overcomes Democrats’ early poor reception to him .

The White House official touted Clayton’s cybersecurity experience as chair of the White House Super Intelligence Force, among other work.

“I’m excited to work more with Kirsten, who has the experience and capabilities needed to help America navigate our increasingly complex and powerful digital infrastructure as our next national cyber director,” Clayton said in a statement. “I look forward to working with the ONCD team to ensure Kirsten has a seamless transition into the role upon her confirmation by the Senate.”

Clayton’s office also had an acting director on loan from another agency prior to his confirmation: Bill Pulte, the director of the Federal Housing Finance Authority, was the acting director of national intelligence from June to August of this year following the departure of Tulsi Gabbard.

Axios first reported the news about Clayton and Davies and their new positions.

business_items.title: CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in network security expansion
business_items.summary: The deal would bring device protection and network access controls under one roof as CrowdStrike seeks a larger role in how companies secure AI agents. The post CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in network security expansion appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
CrowdStrike agreed to acquire Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, combining endpoint and zero-trust network security to protect AI agents.

CrowdStrike said Monday it agreed to acquire Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at about $43.9 billion, giving the cybersecurity company a network security business alongside its software for protecting devices and cloud applications.

The acquisition would bring two kinds of security under one owner: tools that monitor what happens on a device or in a cloud application, and tools that control what those systems can connect to. That distinction matters as employees, applications and artificial intelligence agents connect directly to cloud services without necessarily routing traffic through a company data center. Zscaler’s approach, known as zero trust, checks whether a user or program is authorized to access a specific resource rather than trusting it based on where it connects from.

“The network used to connect people to places. Now it connects agents to data,” CrowdStrike founder and CEO George Kurtz said in the announcement.

Daniel Bernard, CrowdStrike’s chief business officer, said in an interview that “this isn’t a shotgun wedding” and the companies’ years of working together gave them a view of how customers were already using their products to secure AI agents.

“The network really starts on the endpoint, and that’s the genesis of how we view this transaction,” Bernard said. He said CrowdStrike’s software focuses on what an agent does on the device where it runs, while Zscaler’s software sets rules for what the agent can access over the network.

“But now where the agent travels needs to be governed and controlled as well,” he said. Under one owner, CrowdStrike plans to combine device activity and network records so security teams can examine what happened on a device alongside the connections it made. It also plans to sell both sets of products under a single contract, giving it a way to reach about 8,000 Zscaler customers that do not currently buy from CrowdStrike. “We want to be the operating system of security,” Bernard said. He described a platform where security teams could monitor activity and enforce rules across devices, cloud applications and networks, with the goal of providing “consistency and ease of use in managing security.”

Bernard said other software makers would still be able to build tools that work with CrowdStrike’s platform. “This isn’t a play of saying, ‘Hey, the only vendor you need to use in your environment is CrowdStrike,’” he said.

Jay Chaudhry, Zscaler’s founder and CEO, said his company and Crowdstrike “are complementary and this is the natural evolution of our longstanding partnership.” He will continue to lead the Zscaler business and join CrowdStrike’s board after the deal closes.

The purchase is the second acquisition announcement from the company in November. Earlier this month at its European conference, CrowdStrike announced it was buying two artificial intelligence security companies, Fiddler AI and Dreadnode.

Both boards approved the deal unanimously. The companies expect it to close in the second half of CrowdStrike’s 2028 fiscal year, pending approval from Zscaler shareholders and regulators.

business_items.title: Dutch privacy authority urges consumers not to buy ‘pervert glasses’
business_items.summary: The Netherlands' data protection agency said smart wearables violate people's privacy, get information wrong, and can result in unsafe situations.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The Netherlands' data protection agency said smart wearables violate people's privacy, get information wrong, and can result in unsafe situations.

The Dutch Data Protection Authority is urging consumers not to buy AI-enabled camera glasses, warning that they compromise the privacy of nearby bystanders and risk the safety of their users.

The authority, whose recent statement falls just short of an outright ban, said that use of the internet-enabled and always-on glasses to record people in public is “almost always prohibited.”

Critics have dubbed these smart wearables as “pervert glasses” for their propensity to be used to video people without their permission, particularly to harass women. While some glasses have warning lights when users are recording, privacy advocates have argued that these alerts are not clear enough. Some people have even made phone apps capable of detecting nearby smart glasses wearers.

The Dutch data protection authority warned that the glasses also produce wrong results and unsafe results. In one test carried out by the Dutch authority, a pair of unnamed glasses “gave dating advice to an adult who indicated that they are interested in a minor.” The glasses also incorrectly read a medicine label and claimed to have called an ambulance when it had not.

The Dutch government’s advice follows a similar move by the Norwegian government , which in September said it was considering a ban on camera-enabled devices.
