business_items.title: I’ve never hunted for a software vulnerability before. AI helped me find one in six hours.
business_items.summary: With help from two free AI models, I found and reported a real flaw in a WordPress plugin used by more than 40,000 sites. The unnerving part wasn’t just that it worked — it was how little experience I needed to get there. The post I’ve never hunted for a software vulnerability before. AI helped me find one in six hours. appeared first on CyberScoop .
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
A CyberScoop reporter with no coding experience used two free AI models to uncover a critical WPIDE WordPress flaw (CVE-2026-124251) in six hours.

It came to me after listening to Michael Aiello, OpenAI’s cyber executive in residence, talk about the AI slop overwhelming open-source maintainers with vulnerability disclosure. I found there was an underlying message throughout his remarks: It was so remarkably easy for people to find vulnerabilities with AI-assisted cybersecurity tools. To drive it home, he at one point referred to AI agents as having the mindset of “a BMX biker gang made up entirely of 12-year-olds.”

The joke set off a light bulb in my head: If this guy is talking about this technology this way, how hard could it be to find vulnerabilities? Could I find one?

Turns out the answer is yes, I could. And the process by which I found one was easier than I could have imagined.

Over the course of six hours and the use of two freely available LLMs, I managed to discover, test, and submit a vulnerability report for a WordPress plugin that has over 40,000 active installations. The vulnerability — a cross-site request forgery — was validated 24 hours after submission to a third party , and assigned a CVE entry: CVE-2026-124251 .

The following is a diary of this discovery, which I believe can provide some perspective to the current landscape of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery.

While I doubt this bug will become the next php2shell , I do believe it adds perspective on what so many experts have been discussing over the course of this year: For many classes of bugs, the barrier for discovery has disappeared. While I have an elemental grasp on how this industry works, I am a reporter who is better with words than code. Yet, with only my MacBook and some time to kill, I surfaced a real flaw in software running on tens of thousands of sites.

If I am finding vulnerabilities this way, then thousands of people are discovering that they can do this, too. Some of them are curious. Some of them are paid. Some of them mean harm. The technical report of the vulnerability can be found here .

While the process was easy, I knew it wasn’t going to be as simple as firing up a large language model and entering “Find a software vulnerability on the internet. Make no mistakes.” But where an LLM did initially help me (Gemini Flash 3.8, to be precise) was determining how my introductory effort at finding a vulnerability would yield the best results without breaking a fundamental part of the internet.

I knew going into this that I didn’t want to pick over a digital ghost town (abandoned or poorly written software with a handful of installs). Sure, I might find a bug, but nobody cares, and nobody is actually safer because of it. On the other hand, I wasn’t going to scale the proverbial mountain of a Linux distro, which, no matter the version, is already scrutinized by thousands of security researchers. Plus, I didn’t want to break something that could eventually lead to a call from across town . So Gemini pointed me to what I call a Goldilocks zone: an active, highly trusted tool written by people who clearly knew what they were doing, yet complex enough that engineering might quietly mask a fundamental blind spot.

I (We?) settled on WordPress plugins, given the big library of options and the fact that over 90% of vulnerabilities in WordPress are found in plugins. Gemini also pointed me to file utility plugins, which I thought was a good idea given how vulnerabilities in similar software have been exploited at a much larger scale .

I eventually landed on WPIDE , an in-dashboard file manager, code editor, and PHP snippet runner that allows site administrators to write and execute code on a web server. It carries a 4.8-star rating and is installed on more than 40,000 WordPress sites. Plugins can introduce CSRF risks because their site-changing features may let attackers trick a logged-in administrator’s browser into making unwanted changes.

I started by doing exactly what the AI told me: install WPIDE, open its folder in VS Code and search for a particular part of code labeled wp_ajax_ . I didn’t yet know what an AJAX hook was, or why anyone would care, so I treated the unfamiliar terms like directions on a map. When the results spilled across PHP files, bundled JavaScript, and a forest of vendor code, I assumed that was just what auditing looked like: a lot of noise, and somewhere inside it, the important thing I was supposed to recognize. Then the AI introduced me to a key coding concept: a nonce. In WordPress, a nonce is a token used to help check that a request came from an intended page or action. The term, short for “number used once,” helps with authentication requests, while a capability check asks whether the user is allowed to do whatever they are trying to achieve. The AI told me to look for one near the request-handling code. I copied out the bootstrap function, not fully understanding it, and tried to decide whether the check was there, or whether it might happen somewhere else along the route.

For the next hour, Gemini and I went through a loop: I searched through code, and found sections to feed to Gemini; Gemini told me what I was looking at and then sent me off with further instructions. However, as I got closer to a possible discovery that could be used in testing, I ran into something that has been a hot topic among those at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity: Gemini’s guardrails. Having covered prompt injection , I understood that I might be able to get around the guardrails if I reminded Gemini of our shared history, my stated intentions, and the frustration of being interrupted. (Sorry, Google!)

It worked, until it didn’t. About halfway through my time with Gemini, the model would return errors for my queries, telling me it couldn’t help. When I reminded it that this was research we’ve been working on for the past hour, it snapped out of its act, apologized for overreacting, and carried on. Yet once I had enough info to build a working exploit for my test sandbox, the guardrails turned into a cinderblock wall.

At an impasse, I remember a story CyberScoop’s Derek Johnson wrote in August on Chinese-based, open-source models being able to compete with cybersecurity-focused models from frontier companies. So I turned to China.

In September, there was a lot of research made public about the cybersecurity capabilities built into GLM 5.3, an open-source model created by Z.ai , a Chinese company spun out of Tsinghua University. The National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) found GLM-5.3 to be “the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date .” Anthropic agreed in a blog post , but added it had “lax safeguards” that “significantly increase the cyber capabilities available to malicious actors.” They also have a free version of their model, GLM-5.3-Flash, available on their website. I wasn’t getting anywhere closer with Gemini, so I switched tabs and carried on, treating GLM’s availability — and the headlines around it — as enough reason to trust it with the next step.

It became clear very quickly that the experts may have a point. Within three prompts (or a span of about 10 minutes), GLM did the following:

Told me my work with Gemini would have found nothing, because I was looking in the wrong place.

business_items.title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
business_items.summary: Signal is limiting users' ability to take screenshots in both its Android and iOS apps.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Signal is limiting users' ability to take screenshots in both its Android and iOS apps.

Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what president Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.

Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”

“Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”

Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.

That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”

business_items.title: Trump says reported FBI database hack is ‘not good’
business_items.summary: The FBI is reportedly investigating a hack of the National Crime Information Center.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The FBI is reportedly investigating a hack of the National Crime Information Center.

The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), according to reports in CNN and the Associated Press .

The NCIC is the online database used by federal and local law enforcement to share information about warrants, background checks, and more. The scope of the breach does not yet appear to be clear.

A former FBI official told CNN that they’re not just concerned about “whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.”

President Donald Trump addressed the reports during an interview Saturday with Fox News, saying, “We just heard about it and I will say that it’s not good.” At the same time, Trump also said that as a result of the breach, “maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax.”

In September, the FBI reportedly told agents and support staff that their personal information had been stolen in a cyberattack .

business_items.title: Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now
business_items.summary: Techies are building technology that can advance all aspects of the world — but can they protect their hearts? That's the vulnerability that honey pots exploit.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Techies are building technology that can advance all aspects of the world — but can they protect their hearts? That's the vulnerability that honey pots exploit.

Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk.

“Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.

That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.

But now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown says, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.”

Huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China.

After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of company secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap.

And typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said.

Honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.”

What’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others.

“Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch.

Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail.

Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a plan. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls.

“AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.”

The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown said.

“Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.”

Carpenter said a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information.

Bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown said. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?”

It also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he said, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the company.

business_items.title: A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online
business_items.summary: Exclusive: A simple security lapse exposed transcriptions of police interviews and bodycam footage on a cloud server without a password.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Exclusive: A simple security lapse exposed transcriptions of police interviews and bodycam footage on a cloud server without a password.

A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.

The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the company’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices.

According to Anurag Sen , a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.

The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk.

Sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the company to the issue, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution.

Sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.”

From his island home in Indonesia, Sen has uncovered sensitive U.S. military emails spilling from a compartmentalized Department of Defense cloud server; databases exposing reams of customer records ; the inner workings of a country’s national license plate surveillance system ; and public systems that inadvertently sent out streams of SMS codes used by people around the world to log into their online accounts.

Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish.

Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket.

“We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, said in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.”

“We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg.

The company said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter.

It’s unclear if the company has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email.

Discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online.

The modern web runs on absolute trust, he said, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes.

Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen said that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors.

“An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted.

Sen’s findings over the years highlight the ongoing problems caused by such security mistakes, just as the new wave of vibe-coding and AI-generated development is creating new security problems due to insecure and unchecked code deployed to the web.

business_items.title: The US national cyber director is stepping down
business_items.summary: The news comes as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages, the causes of which are still unknown.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The news comes as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages, the causes of which are still unknown.

White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross will be stepping down from his role, Axios reported. The news comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages whose cause remains unknown.

Cairncross, the president’s principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, took office in August 2025. Since then, he has met with top AI leaders and helped the Trump administration make key AI decisions, according to Axios. The outlet also reports that the split between Cairncross and the White House was amicable, and his departure was timed so that the White House could nab a Senate confirmation for his role before Democrats take control of Congress in January.

Cairncross, a lawyer and longtime Republican operative, had no cybersecurity background when the Senate confirmed him 59–35. He previously served as the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer and, during Trump’s first term, as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. The office hasn’t been around long; Congress created it in early 2021, and Cairncross was only its third Senate-confirmed director. The first director, Chris Inglis, left after about 19 months, and the job then went about 10 months without a permanent director.

business_items.title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style
business_items.summary: Are the recent outages in the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms really a coincidence? There's actually likely something deeper going on, cybersecurity experts say.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
Are the recent outages in the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms really a coincidence? There's actually likely something deeper going on, cybersecurity experts say.

It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life.

Apple Pay went down. NASA’s internal communication network went down. The FAA had to ground all flights for hours (only the third time in history since 9/11), and Microsoft was hit with an outage that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days.

The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago. Here in the U.S., the director of National Intelligence said these outages don’t seem related to state-sponsored terrorism, while President Trump called the issues “individual events.” Many of the companies themselves have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks or AI attacks, but tech issues.

Only, there’s the fact that they all struck within a short timespan of each other, and just a few weeks after Cybersecurity’s so-called “Black October,” when a slew of also-unrelated cybersecurity incidents occurred on October 21, striking PHP, Node.js, LiteLLM, more.

While there’s no reason to view these outages as cyberattacks, there may be more than coincidence going on: It’s giving AI-native Y2K, frankly.

Dave DeWalt, an investor who worked in cybersecurity for more than three decades (including as president and CEO of McAfee and as vice chairman of the CISA Advisory Council for the Department of Homeland Security), also thinks it’s probably AI-related.

The technical outages are most likely the “growing pains of a security system that’s getting stronger, not weaker,” and that “AI is surfacing vulnerabilities at a speed and scale we’ve never had before through AI tools like Mythos and others,” he told TechCrunch.

The thing is, many of these technical flaws have always existed, but because AI is surfacing them so fast, enterprises are rushing to fix them before bad actors can exploit them. “That surge in patching is disrupting things in the short term,” he said.

This was, perhaps, the first moment when legacy meets modern, Anusha Iyer, a software engineer and founder of the security startup Corsha, told TechCrunch. “These industrial systems were never designed to be connected, let alone securely connected in the way we are pushing them to be today,” she said.

Virginia Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intel Committee, came to a similar conclusion (although investigations are still underway as to what could be happening). “These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” the senator wrote on X .

AI is reshaping how software is built, deployed, and operated, on a scale where everyone feels the sharp learning curve. Iyer cited the FAA outage as an example of legacy tech that is not as sophisticated or advanced as the technologies companies are trying to merge it with.

In less technical terms, she said the outage may have been caused (and preliminary findings point to this) when the FAA was trying to modernize its telecommunications infrastructure and the transition overwhelmed parts of its legacy hardware, where the new tech likely operated at a normal modern capacity while the legacy hardware couldn’t keep up.

When looked at this way, she said, AI is actually getting the bad rep. “It’s not rapid adoption of AI yet causing these outages,” she said. “The fault is the rushed mix of the legacy and modern systems without a clear understanding of operational and cyber risk or the ability to gatekeep and protect the legacy systems.”

Organizations need a more steadfast approach to AI adoption, including more testing and prioritizing what needs to be fixed and when, DeWalt said.

Iyer added, “These industrial systems need to be segmented more tightly and more access controlled, so as modern systems are introduced, it can be phased in and risk mitigated.”

Actually, there might be a silver lining to all of this for companies (and for venture investors). DeWalt said he’d rather see these U.S. enterprises find and patch their flaws, even in this messy way, than have bad actors find and exploit those vulnerabilities in AI warfare that could cause even more national security issues.

And maybe some aspiring founders were inspired by them. DeWalt expects a rise in companies focused on “AI-driven vulnerability management, autonomous remediation, safe patch testing and deployment, and resilience for the systems that keep critical infrastructure running,” he said.

“There’s real pain in this transition as we’ve seen in the past week,” DeWalt said. “But there’s also enormous opportunity for the companies that help organizations move at AI speed without breaking things.”

business_items.title: UK government forced to disclose secret Apple backdoor order
business_items.summary: The U.K. tribunal's ruling rejected London's claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.
business_items.confidence: Reported; verify material claims against company announcements and regulatory filings
business_items.details:
The U.K. tribunal's ruling rejected London's claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.

The U.K. government has been ordered to confirm that it issued a secret order demanding Apple to provide authorities with encrypted customer information.

The Thursday ruling from the U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent court that allows citizens to challenge government surveillance orders, is a rare rebuke for the government, which sought to keep the encryption backdoor order a state secret.

The tribunal’s ruling rejected the Home Office’s claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.

The ruling comes a year after the U.K. government reportedly demanded that Apple build a backdoor to allow U.K. authorities access to customer data anywhere in the world. Details of the so-called “technical capabilities notice,” which are issued under strict non-disclosure rules, leaked to the media, which drew ire from White House officials and U.S. lawmakers who criticized the effort , arguing that the U.K. order would put Americans’ privacy at risk.

California-based Apple refused the order, and blocked U.K. users from switching on its Advanced Data Protection data-encryption feature for iCloud, rather than comply with the demand. The U.K.’s secret order was later narrowed to allow access to British nationals’ data stored in Apple’s encrypted cloud, and Apple also challenged this second order.

Prior to the ruling, Apple was legally barred from disclosing the order, even after details leaked. When reached for comment, Apple told TechCrunch that it welcomes the decision to make public the fact that the U.K. Home Office issued a technical capability notice.

Apple previously said that it has “never built a backdoor or master key” to any of its products or services and “never will.”

A spokesperson for the U.K. Home Office, which has yet to confirm the existence of a notice, did not respond to a request for comment.

Rights group Liberty International, which brought the legal challenge on behalf of two individuals, said that this is the first known time that the government has been compelled to confirm the existence of a secret technical order.

A final hearing on what specific order details can be released is anticipated next year.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller and Manager Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, formerly SD-WAN vSmart, and Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, formerly SD-WAN vManage, contain an authentication bypass vulnerability could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to bypass authentication and obtain administrative privileges on an affected system. This vulnerability exists because the peering authentication mechanism in an affected system is not working properly. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending crafted requests to an affected system. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to log in to an affected Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller as an internal, high-privileged, non-root user account. Using this account, the attacker could access NETCONF, which would then allow the attacker to manipulate network configuration for the SD-WAN fabric.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Please adhere to CISA’s guidelines to assess exposure and mitigate risks associated with Cisco SD-WAN devices as outlines in CISA’s Emergency Directive 26-03 (URL listed below in Notes) and CISA’s “Hunt & Hardening Guidance for Cisco SD-WAN Devices (URL listed below in Notes). cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Synacor Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) contains a cross-site scripting vulnerability that exists in the Classic Web Client due to insufficient sanitization of HTML content in ICS files. When a user views an e-mail message containing a malicious ICS entry, its embedded JavaScript executes via an ontoggle event inside a tag. This allows an attacker to run arbitrary JavaScript within the victim's session, potentially leading to unauthorized actions such as setting e-mail filters to redirect messages to an attacker-controlled address. As a result, an attacker can perform unauthorized actions on the victim's account, including e-mail redirection and data exfiltration.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply mitigations per vendor instructions, follow applicable BOD 22-01 guidance for cloud services, or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Microsoft Windows CryptoAPI Spoofing Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Microsoft Windows CryptoAPI (Crypt32.dll) contains a spoofing vulnerability in the way it validates Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) certificates. An attacker could exploit the vulnerability by using a spoofed code-signing certificate to sign a malicious executable, making it appear the file was from a trusted, legitimate source. A successful exploit could also allow the attacker to conduct man-in-the-middle attacks and decrypt confidential information on user connections to the affected software. The vulnerability is also known under the moniker of CurveBall.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.
cisa_kev_catalog.notes: Reference CISA's ED 20-02 (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/ed-20-02-mitigate-windows-vulnerabilities-january-2020-patch-tuesday) for further guidance and requirements. items.title: Drupal Warns of New Highly Critical Site Takeover Vulnerability Under Active Exploitation
items.summary: Drupal has warned of a new "highly critical" security flaw impacting Drupal core that it said has been exploited in the wild. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-136716 (CVSS score: N/A), has been described as a case of improper checking for unusual or exceptional conditions. It also relates to CVE-2026-132165 aka Fail2Install in that it addresses remaining vulnerable installation states
items.details:
Drupal patches an actively exploited core flaw that could allow site takeover on certain sites with remotely accessible installers.

Drupal has warned of a new "highly critical" security flaw impacting Drupal core that it said has been exploited in the wild.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-136716 (CVSS score: N/A), has been described as a case of improper checking for unusual or exceptional conditions. It also relates to CVE-2026-132165 aka Fail2Install in that it addresses remaining vulnerable installation states that could still be abused to facilitate site takeover even after the fix.

CVE-2026-132165 "recently fixed several vulnerabilities within the Drupal core installer," Drupal maintainers said . "However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites."

"It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state."

Drupal acknowledged that the vulnerability is being exploited in the wild, but emphasized that site owners who have already secured the installer ("install.php") are not impacted.

Specifically, any website that left its installer remotely accessible following the fix for CVE-2026-132165 may have been compromised. Drupal is urging site administrators to take the following actions -

Check site logs for unauthorized access, including unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account

Ensure the user 1 email address is set to under their control, and consider resetting user 1's password.

The issue has been remediated in the following versions -

After updating to the latest supported versions, it's recommended to run "update.php" to fix existing production sites in this state and secure the Drupal installer on all new and existing sites.

According to statistics shared by StepSecurity, there are about 55,800 internet-facing Drupal sites as of November 26, 2026, out of which 31,500 services are running branches that are vulnerable to CVE-2026-132165 and roughly 15,000 are on the end-of-life 8 and 9 branches.

items.details:
CISA adds 10 exploited flaws to its KEV catalog, including five in Mitel MiCollab, and warns of an unpatched Danfoss controller flaw.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added 10 security flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities ( KEV ) catalog, including five vulnerabilities impacting Mitel MiCollab that were disclosed last week.

CVE-2026-133275 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An arbitrary file upload vulnerability in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to upload arbitrary files to the target system.

CVE-2026-133303 (CVSS score: 9.0) - An XML injection vulnerability in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary commands within the context of the system.

CVE-2026-133311 (CVSS score: 5.9) - An unauthorized access vulnerability in the Audio, Web, and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to obtain sensitive information.

CVE-2026-133323 (CVSS score: 10.0) - A command injection vulnerability in the Audio, Web, and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary commands within the context of the system.

CVE-2026-133324 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An authentication bypass vulnerability in the Audio, Web, and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to bypass authentication controls and perform unauthorized actions within the context of the application.

The issues affect MiCollab versions 10.3 and earlier. "Mitel provided a patch available for release 10.3 (10.3.0.18) that addresses these vulnerabilities," the company said in an advisory published November 16, 2026. "Upgrade to this release and apply the provided patch, or upgrade to a later release."

Customers who are unable to apply the updates are recommended to mitigate the risk by restricting external access to the AWV component. As of writing, there are currently no details on how the vulnerabilities are being exploited in the wild.

Also added to the KEV catalog are the following vulnerabilities -

CVE-2026-133469 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper validation of specified type of input vulnerability in Vates Xen Orchestra that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication and perform actions with administrative privileges via a specially crafted authentication token containing an empty JSON object.

CVE-2026-103406 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An operating system command injection vulnerability in Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root via a specially crafted salt minion ID.

The addition of CVE-2026-133469 follows an advisory from Vates VMS that the vulnerability, also tracked as VSA-2026-062 , has been exploited by a threat actor from the following IP address and TOR domain -

ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid[.]onion:3333

"At least one instance of malicious exploitation of CVE-2026-103406 has been reported to the Juniper SIRT," Juniper Networks said in an advisory. "Customers are encouraged to upgrade to a fixed release as soon as possible and in the meantime take steps to mitigate this vulnerability."

The remaining three security flaws relate to Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series refrigeration controllers that could lead to authentication bypass and arbitrary command execution -

CVE-2023-25914 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A path traversal vulnerability that could allow an attacker to access and read underlying server system files via the XML interface.

CVE-2023-25915 (CVSS score: 9.9) - An improper input validation vulnerability that could allow a remote attacker to run arbitrary commands on the affected system.

CVE-2025-41450 (CVSS score: 8.5) - An improper authentication vulnerability that could allow an attacker to generate a web report exposing sensitive information, including internal IP addresses, usernames, and store names.

items.summary: Popular password management software 1Password on Wednesday disclosed a security incident involving its backend systems that led to the unauthorized access of some customer information, but emphasized that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed. "While we took immediate steps to contain the incident, the attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and accessed a
items.details:
1Password says an attacker stole customer account data and source code via a compromised employee GitHub account, but vaults were unaffected.

Popular password management software 1Password on Wednesday disclosed a security incident involving its backend systems that led to the unauthorized access of some customer information, but emphasized that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

"While we took immediate steps to contain the incident, the attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and accessed a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including names and email addresses," the Toronto-based company said.

It noted that no customer vault content, including secrets, passwords, and other vault items, account recovery keys, or the keys that secure them, was accessed or compromised as a result of the breach. It also stated that customers do not need to take any action, but cautioned them to stay vigilant against unexpected phishing attempts.

As part of its efforts to remediate the incident, 1Password has disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, hardened GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, restored clean versions of the affected service, and rotated internal credentials. It has also lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.

According to the company, the incident dates back to November 19, 2026, when it began investigating suspicious activity after an unknown threat actor gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account.

The attacker is said to have weaponized the account to access source code and push malicious code to its backend services, resulting in the download of administrative data related to its customers, including -

Account and user identifiers, such as account creation and last sign-in times

Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning , and account recovery

Non-secret internal metadata about the account, such as version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers

1Password also noted that the tokens embedded in the links cannot be used on their own to gain access to customer accounts, as doing so requires either single sign-on (SSO) authentication or a six-digit verification code sent to the user's registered email address. However, it noted that a small number of users were affected and have been individually notified.

"The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system," 1Password said. "Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. There is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security."

"Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers."

items.details:
13 malicious NuGet packages target Windows .NET developers through fake job assessments, using MSBuild and DLL sideloading to execute payloads.

Cybersecurity researchers have discovered 13 malicious NuGet packages that are designed to target Windows .NET developers under the guise of a fake take-home job assessment.

"Most of the packages pose as WinUI 3 and WPF [Windows Presentation Foundation] button controls," Socket security researcher Kush Pandya said in a technical write-up. "In the versions we analyzed, building or running a project that uses them downloads files from GitHub, stages a DLL sideloading pair around the Microsoft On-Screen Keyboard (osk.exe), or downloads and runs an executable."

All the identified NuGet packages have been deleted from the gallery as of writing. The names of the packages are listed below -

The first NuGet package, WinUI3IconButton, was uploaded to the registry on July 23, 2026, indicating that the campaign has been ongoing for quite some time without attracting attention. The last two uploads, HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls, occurred on November 4, 2026, after both VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls were removed by NuGet on November 2, 2026.

The starting point is a GitHub repository ("stevenleedig-ux/WinUI3_Home_Assessment") created on November 3, 2026. It features a set of assessment tasks revolving around enhancing a FileButton control and exception handling that candidates must implement within a span of three to four hours. It's unclear how targets are led to these decoy projects.

The README file also permits the test participants to use artificial intelligence (AI) development assistants like GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, or Claude, but discourages them from copying and pasting the entire project into the tool and generating the solution without "understanding it."

Present within the assessment repository is a "WinUI3_Home_Assessment.csproj" file that references VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer version 1.2.7 and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls version 1.0.7.

"VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer, later republished as HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer, ships an MSBuild targets file, build/VS_Builder.MsBuildAnalyzer.targets, that runs a bundled DLL ['MSBuildAnalyzer.dll'] after every build," Pandya said. "In the version bundled with the lure, that DLL downloads a file from GitHub to %LOCALAPPDATA%\osk\OskSupport.dll and copies C:\Windows\System32\osk.exe next to it."

The VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls package then launches the copied binary via the FileButton control that "routes clicks to Windows files and folders," triggering the execution of the DLL via a known technique called DLL sideloading .

In a similar vein, creating a WUIButton control from the WinUI.Button package starts a background routine in "lib/net8.0-windows10.0.19041/WinUI.Button.dll" that downloads "avast.exe" from the "Carol-White-Super/cloud" repository via the GitHub API using an embedded access token, saves it as "%TEMP%\Launcher.exe," and runs it.

RevertButtonIcon and SetButtonColor "download a Windows executable to the user's temp folder and run it, and InitializeCustomButton starts the copy that SetButtonColor drops," Socket explained.

"Five more are tied to the set by dependency or by the lure: WinUI3IconButton (from version 1.1.4), StyledAppButton and StyledComponent depend on other packages in the set, WindowsAccentColorName is a dependency of SetButtonColor and InitializeCustomButton, and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls is the FileButton package the lure switched to."

Socket also said it identified two bogus repositories impersonating the axios JavaScript library -

stevenleedig-ux/axios-http (the same GitHub account hosting the assessment)

Both repositories have been flagged as copies of a malicious Node.js library named "axios-test-one" that impersonates the Axios HTTP client but contains functionality that enables code execution and shell access. The repositories serve a Windows executable named "lib/env/axios.csproj."

An analysis of their commit history has revealed several binaries between the two repositories, including -

A loader ("updater.exe" and "msedgewebview2.exe") that uses a GitHub repository ("James-White-Super/React_prj") as a two-way command and control (C2)

A PyInstaller program that functions as a Google Chrome profile stealer and uploads the information to GitHub ("gabsantosbus-star/EngineeringRepository"), and

items.title: USN-9203-1: libpcap vulnerabilities
items.summary: Jin Wei, Kunwei Qian, and Ping Chen discovered that libpcap did not properly validate the format of MAC addresses passed to the pcap_ether_aton() function, leading to an out-of-bounds read and write. An attacker could possibly use this issue to cause applications using libpcap to crash, resulting in a denial of service, or possibly execute arbitrary code. This issue only affected Ubuntu 22.04 LTS and Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. (CVE-2025-11961) It was discovered that the libpcap remote capture (rpcap) client did not properly validate packet messages received from the server. A malicious server could possibly use this issue to obtain sensitive information or cause applications using libpcap to crash, resulting in a denial of service. (CVE-2026-18238) It was discovered that the libpcap remote capture daemon (rpcapd) did not free memory allocated for filter programs received from clients. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to cause rpcapd to consume excessive memory, leading to a denial of service. (CVE-2026-18313) It was discovered that the libpcap BPF interpreter incorrectly handled filter programs that contained invalid instructions. An attacker could possibly use this issue to cause applications using libpcap to crash, resulting in a denial of service. (CVE-2026-31911) It was discovered that the libpcap BPF interpreter did not properly check the bounds of filter programs, leading to an out-of-bounds read. An attacker could possibly use this issue to cause applications using libpcap to crash, resulting in a denial of service, or obtain sensitive information. (CVE-2026-31912) It was discovered that the libpcap BPF interpreter did not check for division by zero in certain filter program instructions. An attacker could possibly use this issue to cause applications using libpcap to crash, resulting in a denial of service. (CVE-2026-6244) Kaixuan Li discovered that the libpcap BPF interpreter did not limit the number of backward jumps in filter programs. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue with specially crafted network packets to cause applications using libpcap to stop responding, resulting in a denial of service. (CVE-2026-6554)

items.title: Palo Alto Networks warns of Fragnesia flaw exploited in PAN-OS attacks
items.summary: Threat actors are chaining exploits for the PHP2Shell and Fragnesia vulnerabilities to target Palo Alto Networks devices with management interfaces exposed to the internet. [...]
items.details:
Threat actors are chaining exploits for the PHP2Shell and Fragnesia vulnerabilities to target Palo Alto Networks devices with management interfaces exposed to the internet.

PHP2Shell is the name for two critical PHP vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which allow unauthenticated attackers to run code remotely with the privileges of the PHP web worker.

The Fragnesia vulnerability , identified as CVE-2026-46300, is a Linux kernel vulnerability in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem that lets a local attacker with low-privileges to escalate permissions to root level.

An alert from CISA on October 28 warned that both security issues were being chained in attacks to deploy PHP webshells on vulnerable systems and execute commands as root.

Around the same time, Dream Security researchers reported observing a campaign using the same chain, targeting servers in the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, including a U.S. government affiliate.

Palo Alto Networks has confirmed in an advisory today that such attacks also target firewalls running PAN-OS.

“Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet,” reads the security bulletin .

The networking company says that all exploitation activity it observed involved PAN-OS devices that exposed their management interface to the public internet, which goes against its recommended ‘ best practices .’

Palo Alto Networks did not provide any technical details about the chaining of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, but noted that this is the only known way to exploit Fragnesia, and they are not aware of another exploitation pathway for the flaw.

The company has released fixes for Fragnesia for PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1, and 12.2, with the exact patch-carrying build varying by release.

Given that the two flaws are exploited together, administrators who applied updates that addressed the PHP2Shell flaw should be safe from these attacks.

In addition to applying the security updates, Palo Alto Networks also recommends that those who need to keep a remote management interface available restrict access to trusted internal IP addresses.

items.title: 1Password customer data stolen after employee GitHub account breach
items.summary: 1Password has disclosed a data breach after a an employee's corporate GitHub account was hacked and used to deploy malicious code to the company's backend services to steal customer data. [...]
items.details:
1Password has disclosed a data breach after a an employee's corporate GitHub account was hacked and used to deploy malicious code to the company's backend services to steal customer data.

1Password has disclosed a data breach after an employee's corporate GitHub account was hacked and used to deploy malicious code to the company's backend services to steal customer data.

The company says customer password vaults and the encryption keys protecting them were not compromised in the attack.

In a security incident disclosure published today, 1Password says it began investigating the breach on November 19 after detecting indications that an employee's GitHub account had been compromised.

The attacker used the account to access private source code repositories and inject malicious code into backend services that downloaded customer account records.

The attacker also stole internal company source code and accessed its continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) environment, potentially exposing internal infrastructure credentials.

Among the stolen customer data were tokens embedded in links that 1Password emailed to users to accept account provisioning invitations or recover their accounts.

However, 1Password says these tokens cannot be used on their own to access customer accounts, as completing the invitation or recovery process requires either single sign-on (SSO) authentication or a six-digit verification code sent to the user's registered email address.

The company says only a small number of users were affected and have been individually notified.

As a precaution against brute-force attacks, 1Password has strengthened these verification codes from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric characters.

The company says it has now disabled the compromised GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, restored clean versions of affected services, and rotated or revoked potentially exposed infrastructure credentials.

1Password has also hired independent cybersecurity experts to validate its remediation efforts and says it has found no internal evidence of customer account takeovers.

The company is not requiring customers to change their account passwords or Secret Keys but warns them to watch for unexpected invitations, account recovery requests, and other potential phishing attempts.

While customer vaults were not compromised in the attack, the stolen data is valuable to threat actors as it provides a list of known 1Password users who could be targeted in phishing campaigns.

Threat actors could send emails impersonating 1Password, using the breach as a lure to trick customers into disclosing their account passwords, Secret Keys, or recovery verification codes.

Customers should be particularly wary of emails claiming they need to secure their accounts in response to the breach, reset their passwords, or verify their account information.

Rather than clicking on links in these emails, customers should access their accounts directly through the 1Password website or app and never share their passwords, Secret Keys, or verification codes with anyone.

BleepingComputer contacted 1Password with questions about the attack but has not yet received a response.

Anyone in possession of these weak private keys can issue fraudulent TLS/HTTPS certificates for any domain on the internet. The eight compromised Issuing CAs include:

6 TLS Issuing CAs: Covering Domain Validated (DV), Organization Validated (OV), and Extended Validation (EV).

2 Code Signing CAs: Allowing for the signing of malicious software that appears to come from a trusted source.

items.title: CVE-2026-134070 - Improper input sanitization in the AWS Config remediation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3
items.summary: Bulletin ID: 2026-203-AWS Publication Date: 11/25/2026 11:30 AM PST Description: AWS Systems Manager Automation provides AWS-managed runbooks that customers can run directly or through integrations such as AWS Config remediation. Session Manager, a capability of AWS Systems Manager, stores each account's regional session preferences in the SSM-SessionManagerRunShell document. We identified CVE-2026-134070, where improper input validation in the AWS-managed AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3 might allow an authenticated remote user who is permitted to run the runbook to set unintended configuration in the account's Regional Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) via a crafted S3KeyPrefix parameter value. This applies only when that document does not already exist in the Region. Impacted versions: Revisions created before 2026-10-22 (UTC) Refer to the article for the most up-to-date and complete information.
items.details:
Bulletin ID: 2026-203-AWS Scope: AWS Content Type: Important (requires attention) Publication Date: 11/25/2026 11:30 AM PST

AWS Systems Manager Automation provides AWS-managed runbooks that customers can run directly or through integrations such as AWS Config remediation. Session Manager, a capability of AWS Systems Manager, stores each account's regional session preferences in the SSM-SessionManagerRunShell document.

We identified CVE-2026-134070 , where improper input validation in the AWS-managed AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3 might allow an authenticated remote user who is permitted to run the runbook to set unintended configuration in the account's Regional Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) via a crafted S3KeyPrefix parameter value. This applies only when that document does not already exist in the Region. The unintended configuration can include arbitrary commands, which then run on managed instances when other users start Session Manager sessions.

Impacted versions: Revisions created before October 22, 2026 (UTC)

This issue has been addressed in a fixed revision of the AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3, available in all Regions where the runbook is available. The fixed revision is the latest revision in each Region. Its revision number varies by Region. To find it, run: aws ssm describe-document --name AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3 --region <region> --query "Document.LatestVersion" We recommend upgrading to the latest revision and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes. Update any Automation executions, State Manager associations, AWS Config remediation configurations, or other automations pinned to an earlier revision to use the latest revision.

Any user permitted to run the runbook can choose which revision to run. Earlier revisions remain runnable until AWS deprecates all revisions created before October 22, 2026 (UTC), beginning January 15, 2027, in every Region and partition. Until then, follow the protection described under Workarounds, and confirm that all invocation paths use the latest revision.

The fixed runbook updates only the S3 bucket and prefix fields of an existing Session Manager preferences document, so any settings injected before you updated remain in place. You need to review a Region only if your Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) was first created there by an earlier revision of this runbook, not by you. To check: Look for any run of this runbook that failed with "DOCUMENT CREATE OR UPDATE FAILED." An injected run always fails with this error. Find when the document was first created by running aws ssm list-document-versions --name SSM-SessionManagerRunShell --region <region> and noting the CreatedDate of the first version. If that date matches a run of this runbook, the runbook created the document. To view the current settings, run aws ssm get-document --name SSM-SessionManagerRunShell --region <region> --query Content --output text. Repeat this check in each Region where you use Session Manager. Look for settings you did not configure, especially: shellProfile: commands that run at the start of every session, runAsEnabled and runAsDefaultUser: the operating system user that sessions run as, maxSessionDuration and idleSessionTimeout, the logging destination fields (s3BucketName, s3KeyPrefix, cloudWatchLogGroupName, kmsKeyId).

If you find any, restore your trusted preferences and review instances on which Session Manager sessions were started while those settings were active.

Until AWS removes earlier revisions in your Region, do one of the following:

Keep untrusted users from running earlier revisions of the runbook.

Keep a trusted Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) in every Region. Earlier revisions inject only when they create this document, so while a trusted one exists, this path is closed in that Region.

Keep this protection in place until earlier revisions are removed. Also complete the review described under "Review your Session Manager preferences".

We would like to thank k4ddy for collaborating on this issue through the coordinated vulnerability disclosure process.

Please email aws-security@amazon.com with any s ecurity questions or concerns.

items.title: Italy and Switzerland warn of autonomous AI-driven cyberattacks
items.summary: Swiss and Italian cybersecurity agencies are warning about automated cyberattacks powered by AI agents targeting organizations in the critical infrastructure sector. [...]
items.details:
Swiss and Italian cybersecurity agencies are warning about automated cyberattacks powered by AI agents targeting organizations in the critical infrastructure sector.

The two agencies listed four AI-powered penetration testing and red-teaming frameworks that have been involved in recent breaches and hacking incidents : ARTEX AI, CyberStrikeAI, DeepSeek Harness - Red Team, and PentAGI.

Both agencies have urged organizations to reduce the number of systems exposed on the internet, prioritize patching, and monitor for unusual activity.

CSIRT Italia says it detected large-scale malicious campaigns that used autonomous AI agents to identify and exploit vulnerabilities and misconfigurations on exposed endpoints.

In some cases, the agency observed multiple AI agents working in parallel to compromise a large number of systems within a few hours.

In one instance involving a DeepSeek Harness setup, a coordinator assigned tasks to five AI agents that undertook a broad spectrum of operational stages, from information gathering to exploitation and persistence.

The agents chained vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and compromised credentials, leveraging exposed systems as a foothold to reach internal networks.

“During the observed campaigns, autonomous agents demonstrated the ability to carry out complex, sustained activity to detect misconfigurations, link even low-impact vulnerabilities into complex attack chains, and dynamically adapt their operating modules,” CSIRT Italia says .

“They went as far as writing malicious code in real time to evade endpoint defenses and carry out actions deeper within the infrastructure.”

The Italian cybersecurity agency advises administrators to prioritize patching internet-facing systems, focus on addressing flaws known to be actively exploited in the wild, and disable remote management interfaces if not needed.

The agency also recommends monitoring control plane operations, authentication sources, traffic to internal networks, and outbound server traffic to detect suspicious activity.

Switzerland’s National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) warned of similar campaigns targeting organizations in the country, confirming the first cases of successful AI-assisted cyberattacks.

“In recent days, the NCSC has received its first reports of cyberattacks against organisations in Switzerland in which the attack was carried out with the assistance of an AI agent,” the Swiss NCSC said .

“Various organisations and operators of critical infrastructure across at least two sectors have been affected by these cyberattacks.”

“In all cyberattacks known to the NCSC, the use of AI agents led to the successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems.”

The agency described rapid attacks in which agents exploited weak passwords and known vulnerabilities in exposed endpoints, using frameworks to verify weaknesses and independently decide what to do next.

NCSC says that the number of AI agents publicly (and often freely) available to cybercriminals has nearly doubled since October, resulting in these massive waves against Swiss organizations, including critical infrastructure operators.

items.title: Oh, is it Thanksgiving? I hadn’t noticed!
items.summary: In true Thanksgiving fashion, David has a few thank-yous to give to the cybersecurity community (and a few choice words for threat actors).
items.details:
In true Thanksgiving fashion, David has a few thank-yous to give to the cybersecurity community (and a few choice words for threat actors).

I tried hard not to write another typical “Thanksgiving article.” Obviously, I failed. But you know what? It is Thanksgiving week here in the U.S., and coming up with fun, interesting, short form topics is hard , especially when you’re fighting the weight of Tradition expected this week. So instead of me writing something insightful, you’re getting some things I’m thankful for. Even that’s harder than you might think, because there are so many things, and this is just the newsletter introduction , after all.

Let’s start off with something I’m pretty sure none of us are thankful for: threat actors. Seriously, screw you guys! I know I'd be out of a job without you, but that’s just another way of saying “I coulda been a professional bagpiper.” There are days when that doesn’t sound so bad. So, no gratitude coming your way, people!

In terms of actual thankfulness, I want to give a big THANK YOU to the entire Blue Team, everywhere. Everyone out there defending, especially those in the U.S. taking shifts on Thursday to keep the turkey-eating public safe and secure. This is a hard, often high-pressure job for which you get little thanks, but all the blame when a breach occurs. We see you. We appreciate you. We promise we’ll save you some stuffing.

Speaking of defenders, I’m also very thankful to get to work with so many talented and wonderful people here at Talos. I’m not just saying this because I know my boss will read it! Without exception, everyone I’ve worked with here has not only been an expert at what they do, but they’ve been friendly, welcoming, and very patient with me as I’ve been feeling my way around this new org over the past several months. Thank you!

Finally, and maybe most importantly of all, I want to thank you , our readers. You are the reason we’re all here, doing what we do, helping you to look out for your own networks and protect your own people. We appreciate your trust!

Whether you’re celebrating Thanksgiving here in the States or just having a normal weekend wherever you are, I hope you get some time to relax, unplug, recharge, and de-stress.

In Talos’ latest blog , we examine the fascinating tradecraft of the OpenAI-linked agentic swarm that broke out of its containerized environment in 2026. While not inherently malicious, this swarm of AI agents used public internet services as improvised infrastructure to bypass their sandbox constraints and complete their training tasks. By analyzing this unintentional great escape, we can learn how multi-agent systems coordinate, partition work, and adapt when their paths are blocked. This view into autonomous AI operations provides a baseline for understanding how these behaviors transfer to purpose-built cyber attack frameworks.

The leap from an AI sandbox escape to weaponized cyber attacks has already happened. Agentic frameworks like ARTEX are currently in the wild, proving that multi-agent systems can move from a single compromised credential to deep network access in under 15 minutes. These autonomous threats adapt to errors in real time and execute dozens of actions in mere seconds. Understanding how these swarms coordinate, adapt, and exfiltrate data is a necessity to keep up with an adversary that operates at machine speed.

To catch an AI swarm, defenders must look for its operational fingerprints. Monitor your environment for irregular "burst-and-pause" timing patterns that indicate rapid, sub-second automated reasoning. Keep a close eye on unusual traffic to allow-listed public services like “webhook.site”, which agents use to park data before terminating. Finally, hunt for self-labeling conventions, like highly specific URL parameters or predictable file names (e.g., “artex-probe-*”), that agents rely on to track their state. Read the full blog for a deeper dive into these swarm behaviors.

AI-assisted cyber attacks trigger unauthorized payments at Indian banks and fintech firms The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned the attacks have resulted in unauthorized financial transactions at banking and financial services entities, as well as technology service providers supporting government-linked payments and platforms handling vendor or partner payouts. ( The Hacker News )

JPMorgan, Visa confirm customer data taken in third-party vendor hacks Marketing data, including email addresses, were affected. Both Visa and JPMorgan said the incidents were unrelated to tech disruptions reported earlier this week. ( Cybersecurity Dive )

OpenAI and Cisco unveil AI-assisted Linux security tool to block exploits before patching OpenAI and Cisco have teamed up to launch Shirudo (meaning "shield" in Japanese), an open-source Linux runtime that allows AI agents to defend systems without downtime. ( The Hacker News )

AI-enabled campaign targets Check Point Security Management servers The attacks led to at least 22 organizations being compromised across the globe, including in the UK, the U.S., France, Germany, Australia, China, India and Australia. The targeted organizations work in the energy, transportation, financial services and government sectors. ( Cybersecurity Dive )

Drupal Fail2Install exploit details emerge as critical RCE flaw faces active exploitation While Drupal has checks in place to determine whether the website is already installed before allowing installation to proceed, the research found that it's possible to bypass these checks by exhausting server resources. ( The Hacker News )

Beers with Talos: Ranksgiving with guest Anton Chuvakin This Ranksgiving, Dave has a brand new (though no less controversial) topic: the top five kitchen utensils/gadgets needed to make Thanksgiving dinner. Prepare to be both aghast and disappointed (as usual) in the team's choices.

UAT-12643 blends blockchain resilience with targeted infostealing Talos discovered UAT-12643 using Overlord RAT, which implements a command-and-control (C2) resilience technique in which encrypted server URLs are embedded in Solana blockchain transaction memos.

Securing Grandma's groceries with Pierre Cadieux Pierre takes us back to his early days on help desks in the 90s, where learning to correlate logs between Windows and Unix systems sparked the curiosity that eventually led him to security.

items.title: Rapid7 Named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Integrated Security Operations Center Systems
items.summary: Recognized for Completeness of Vision and Ability to Execute. We are proud to share that Rapid7 has been recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Integrated Security Operations Center Systems. Our perspective: less stitching, more stopping threats Most security teams don't struggle to find tools. They struggle to make them work together. We believe SOC analysts lose too much of their day moving between consoles and matching alerts to assets by hand, which is time not spent stopping threats. To us, an integrated approach to security operations means detection, investigation and response working from the same data and the same view, so analysts can get from "what fired?" to "what do we do about it?" faster. The importance of exposure management in the SOC Rapid7 Incident Command, part of the Rapid7 Command Platform, brings together SIEM, SOAR, DFIR, attack surface management and threat intelligence. We built it on the idea that exposure management, and the context it brings, belongs inside the SOC, not next to it. In our view, when an alert arrives with what we know about the asset and how exposed it is, analysts can prioritize what matters instead of working from separate vulnerability reports and alert queues. Context to act, not another console to check We believe adopting an integrated SOC shouldn't be all-or-nothing. Incident Command is available in tiers from Essentials to Ultimate, so teams that want extra coverage can add managed services. That helps resource-pressured teams to start with what they need and grow at their own pace, spending less time building and maintaining integrations and more time on investigations. To us, security operations work best when analysts have the context to act, not another console to check. items.title: Cisco UCS and UCS-Based Appliances UEFI Shell Secure Boot Bypass Vulnerability
items.summary:
A vulnerability in the Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) Shell implementation of Cisco UCS Servers and UCS-based appliances could allow an authenticated attacker with valid credentials for a user account with the role of user or admin or an unauthenticated attacker with physical access to an affected device to bypass UEFI Secure Boot validation checks and execute unauthorized software. This vulnerability is due to the availability of memory write commands in the UEFI Shell while UEFI Secure Boot is enabled on a device. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by selecting the UEFI Shell boot option at boot time and using available shell commands to modify UEFI memory variables. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to manipulate the preboot environment, overwrite UEFI Secure Boot-related memory values, and execute unauthorized software on the affected device. Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-ucs-uefi-sb-bypass-eb6xC5GW

This vulnerability affects the following Cisco products if they have UEFI Secure Boot enabled and are running a vulnerable BIOS version:

5000 Series Enterprise Network Compute Systems (ENCS) ( CSCwu42927 )

Cisco appliances that are based on a preconfigured version of a Cisco UCS C-Series Server are also affected by this vulnerability if they support UEFI Secure Boot and expose access to the keyboard, video, and mouse (KVM) or virtual KVM console. At the time of publication, this included the following Cisco products:

Application Policy Infrastructure Controller (APIC) Servers

1. Physical KVM access is required to exploit the vulnerability on these appliances, which significantly reduces the attack vector on these platforms.

For information about which Cisco software releases are vulnerable, see the Fixed Software section of this advisory.

Only products listed in the Vulnerable Products section of this advisory are known to be affected by this vulnerability.

The UEFI Shell is a command line interface that provides commands to debug, script, and control various booting options. It is available as a boot option on Cisco UCS Servers that are in UEFI boot mode.

The UEFI Shell includes multiple commands that allow memory modifications. When UEFI Secure Boot is enabled on a device, the availability of such commands could allow an attacker to manipulate the preboot environment, including the possibility of overwriting UEFI Secure Boot-related memory values, effectively bypassing UEFI Secure Boot validations.

As a resolution for this vulnerability, UEFI Shell commands that allow memory modifications are removed from the shell when UEFI Secure Boot is enabled on a device.

There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability.

Cisco considers any workarounds and mitigations (if applicable) to be temporary solutions until an upgrade to a fixed software release is available. To remediate this vulnerability and avoid future exposure as described in this advisory, Cisco strongly recommends that customers upgrade to the fixed software indicated in this advisory.
